en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on the Buddha, concerning the Question on Inference.
6. The Question on the Arahant’s Experience of Feeling “Venerable Nāgasena, you say:
‘An Arahant experiences one kind of feeling—the bodily, not the mental.’”

“Venerable Nāgasena, is it not the case that the mind of an Arahant, whatever body it depends upon for its occurrence, therein the Arahant is without mastery, without ownership, and lacks sovereign power?
“Yes, Great King.
“But Venerable Nāgasena, this is not logical: that he should be without mastery, without ownership, and lacking sovereign power over his own mind while it occurs within the body.”
“Even a bird, Bhante, is the master, the lord, and the one who exercises power over the very nest where it dwells.
“Great King, there are these ten qualities that follow the body, running after and revolving around the body from birth to birth.
Which ten?”
“Cold, heat, hunger, thirst, excrement, urine, drowsiness, old age, sickness, and death—these, O Great King, are the ten things that follow the body;
in birth after birth they run along with and revolve around the body. In this regard, the Arahant is without mastery, without ownership, and lacks authority over them.
“Venerable Nāgasena, for what reason does command or sovereignty not operate within the body of an Arahant? Tell me the reason for this.”

“Great king, just as whatever beings depend upon the earth all move, dwell, and maintain their livelihood depending on the earth—do these beings exercise command over the earth, or do they possess sovereignty over it?
“No, venerable sir.
“In the same way, great king, the mind of an arahant proceeds depending on the body, yet the arahant exercises no command over the body, nor does he possess sovereignty over it.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, for what reason does an ordinary person experience both bodily and mental feeling?
“Because his mind has not been developed, Great King, the ordinary person experiences both bodily and mental feeling.

Just as, Great King, a hungry and distressed ox might be tied to a weak, fragile, and small blade of grass or to a creeper; when that ox becomes enraged, it breaks away from its tether along with the thing to which it was bound.”
“In the same way, great king, for one whose mind is undeveloped, feeling arises and agitates the mind; the agitated mind tosses and turns the body, causing it to writhe and roll about.
Then that person of undeveloped mind trembles, cries out, and utters fearful shrieks. This, great king, is the reason why an ordinary person experiences both bodily and mental feeling.
“But what is the reason, by which reason an Arahant experiences only one kind of feeling—the bodily—and not the mental?”
“Great King, the mind of an Arahant is developed, well-developed, tamed, well-tamed, obedient, and compliant.
When he is touched by painful feeling, he firmly grasps it as ‘impermanent,’ and he binds his mind to the pillar of concentration.
His mind, being bound to that pillar of concentration, neither trembles nor wavers.”
"It remains steady and undistracted; through the expansion of the transformation of his feelings, his body bends, stretches, and turns over.
This, Great King, is the reason why an Arahant experiences only one kind of feeling—the bodily—and not the mental.
"Venerable Nāgasena, that indeed is a marvel in the world: that while the body moves, the mind does not move. Tell me the reason for this."
“Great king, just as when a great, massive tree is endowed with trunk, branches, and foliage, and its branches shake when struck by the force of the wind, would its trunk also shake?
“No, venerable sir.
“In the same way, great king, when an arahant is touched by painful feeling, he firmly [contemplates it] as ‘impermanent.’”
He grasps it and fixes his mind upon the pillar of concentration. As his mind is fixed upon that pillar of concentration, it does not tremble or waver;

it becomes steady and undistracted. Through the expansion of the transformation of his feelings, his body bends, stretches, and turns over, yet his mind does not tremble or waver; [his] aggregate remains firm.
“...like that of a great tree.
“It is wonderful, venerable Nāgasena! It is marvelous, venerable Nāgasena! Never before have I seen such a perpetual lamp of the Dhamma.
This is the sixth dilemma: on the experience of feelings by an Arahant.
